topics.title: What a secondary dominant is
topics.summary: The V–I relation is so strong (overtone series: P5 and P8 above the bass) that a dominant can make any major or minor triad sound like a temporary tonic: tonicization. Primary dominants (V) belong to the key; secondary dominants come from outside it, so they are chromatic (altered) chords. Both have dominant function.

terms.def: make a chord sound like a temporary tonic
a chord with accidentals not in the key signature
read "five of …": the slash names the chord being tonicized

rules: Only major and minor triads can be tonicized (never a diminished triad).

topics.title: Spelling and analysing secondary dominants
topics.summary: Two short procedures: one to write the chord, one to recognise it.
rules: Spelling: 1. Name the root of the chord to be tonicized. 2. Go up a P5. 3. Build a major triad (V) or Mm7 (V7) on that note.
Analysis: 1. Write the lead-sheet symbol. 2. Is the altered chord M or Mm7? 3. Go down a P5. 4. Would a major/minor triad on that note be diatonic? If yes, the chord is V(7) of it.

topics.title: Secondary dominants in progressions
topics.summary: Insert a secondary dominant in front of its target in the harmonic-progression chart; secondary dominants can be chained, and they can resolve deceptively.
rules: Voice-lead secondary dominants exactly like primary dominants: chordal 7th down, temporary leading tone up.
Exception: the temporary leading tone MAY go down a half step when it becomes the 7th of the next (tonicizing) chord — this makes a descending chromatic line.

topics.title: Secondary leading-tone chords
topics.summary: A leading-tone chord (vii°, vii°7, viiø7) can also tonicize a chord. Use the fully diminished forms for minor targets; major targets can take either.
rules: Major target: vii°7/□ or viiø7/□. Minor target: vii°7/□ or vii°/□.
In minor keys some of these are diatonic: vii°7/III and viiø7/III are just ii° and iiø7; viiø7/V does not occur in natural minor (use vii°7/V).
Spelling: 1. Name the root of the chord to be tonicized. 2. Go down a m2. 3. Build vii°, viiø7 or vii°7 on that note.
Analysis: 1. Is the altered chord °, ø7 or °7? 2. Name the note a m2 above its root. 3. Would a M/m triad on that note be diatonic?
Voice leading as usual: chordal 7th down, leading tone up.
guidelines: Insert secondary LT chords in the progression chart like secondary dominants (e.g. vi – viiø7/V → I6/4 – V – I).

topics.title: Enharmonic spelling follows resolution
topics.summary: Spell a chromatic note by where it goes: sharps resolve up, flats resolve down. A note spelled with the wrong accidental gives a wrong analysis.
rules: ♯ resolves up; ♭ resolves down.

topics.title: Secondary deceptive resolutions and nested functions
topics.summary: A secondary dominant can resolve deceptively: V7/vi → IV (the VI of vi) instead of vi. Secondary functions can also be nested (vii°7/V/vi → V7/vi). Uncommon secondary deceptive resolutions go somewhere unexpected; there, smooth voice leading matters more than the progression chart.

topics.title: Secondary functions that modulate
topics.summary: A string of secondary chords that is confirmed by its own cadence becomes a short (temporary) modulation. Changing between inversions of the same chord without resolving is allowed.

topics.title: Modulation vs. tonicization; key relationships
topics.summary: Modulation is a shift of tonal centre within a movement, often used to articulate form. Tonicization is short (1–2 chords) and has no cadence in the new key; modulation is longer and is confirmed by a cadence.
rules: Enharmonically equivalent keys (C♯/D♭) and parallel keys (C major / C minor) share the same tonic — moving between them is NOT modulation.

topics.title: Common-chord (pivot) modulation
topics.summary: Find a chord that belongs to both keys and use it as the hinge.
rules: Writing: 1. Write the lead-sheet symbols of both keys. 2. Find the chords common to both keys.
Analysis: 1. Find the point of modulation — the first chord that belongs only to the new key, or a I6/4 in the new key. 2. Go back one chord and check whether it is a pivot (common chord).
guidelines: iii and vi are rarely inverted (a sign the analysis should switch keys).
Altered chords can pivot too: a secondary V(7) or vii°(7) may be a secondary function in either or both keys.

topics.title: Sequential, common-tone, monophonic and direct modulation
topics.summary: Other ways to change key, from smoothest to most abrupt.

a passage is repeated a step (or a 3rd, or a 5th) higher/lower, harmonically and melodically; with or without a common chord

a single held note links the keys; dramatic, "suspended"; often chromatic-mediant relations (Mozart, Beethoven)
a single melodic line changes key (Bach violin partitas, cello suites; jazz improvisation)
A♯ (leading tone of b) → A♮: b → D
no smoothing: the new phrase simply starts in the new key; rarely inside a phrase (Bach, at a fermata)
like a sequential modulation without repeating the progression

topics.title: Mode mixture (borrowed chords)
topics.summary: Mixture borrows notes from the parallel mode: a major key takes ♭3̂, ♭6̂ and ♭7̂ from its parallel minor; a minor key takes ♮3̂ (and ♮6̂, ♮7̂) — most famously the major tonic at the end (Picardy third).
rules: Voice-lead borrowed notes smoothly: approach ♭6̂ by step and resolve it down by step (♭6̂ → 5̂).
guidelines: Controversy: is a passage mixture or a move to the parallel minor (modulation)?

Why does the major triad sound more stable than the minor? The major triad's intervals reinforce the root's overtones (all consonant with the fundamental); the minor 3rd implies a different fundamental (A♭ under C–E♭). Acoustics, psychology, philosophy all play a part.

topics.title: The Neapolitan chord (♭II, N)
topics.summary: An 18th-century colour associated with Naples (e.g. Cimarosa): a major triad on lowered 2̂. Most common in minor, possible in major. It works as a subdominant (predominant), like IV or ii.
rules: Use it mostly as N6 (first inversion); N6/4 is rare.
Double the bass of N6.
♭2̂ resolves down, usually to the leading tone.
Exception to the no-augmented/diminished-leap rule: ♭2̂ may move to 7̂ by a diminished 3rd.
guidelines: Typical path: (i, iv or ii°6) → [V(7) of N] → N6 → [vii°7/V] → (i6/4) V.
The d3 (♭2̂ → 7̂) is often filled in with a passing 1̂.

topics.title: Spelling augmented-sixth chords
topics.summary: Augmented-sixth "chords" are really sonorities: they arise from smooth linear voice leading toward 5̂ (or to the cadential 6/4), so they are named by type, not by root.
rules: 1. Pick the scale degree to approach (5̂ for the standard types).
2. Bass = a m2 above it (♭6̂ in major, 6̂ in minor).
3. Upper voice = a m2 below it, written up the octave (♯4̂). Bass + this voice = the augmented 6th.
4. Add the M3 above the bass (1̂). Steps 2–4 make the Italian core.
5. Choose the type: Italian (It+6) — double the M3 above the bass; French (Fr+6) — add the A4 above the bass (2̂); German (Ger+6) — add the P5 above the bass (♭3̂).
guidelines: Style association: Italian — opera; French — colourful; German — sturdy.
They are built on a bass position, not a root, so they have no "inversions"; any member of an It+6 may appear in the bass, and the bass position does not need to be indicated.

topics.title: Augmented sixths: progression and resolution
topics.summary: Augmented-sixth sonorities have dominant-preparation function: they usually come right before V or the cadential I(i)6/4. The A6 expands outward to an octave.
rules: The A6 resolves by expanding to a P8 (♭6̂ down to 5̂, ♯4̂ up to 5̂).
Ger+6 goes to I(i)6/4 (not straight to V) to avoid parallel 5ths.
Exception: before a secondary dominant of V (V4/3/V or vii°6/5/V) the A6 moves to a M6 with smooth voice leading (step and common tone).
guidelines: As a neighbour chord: V → +6 → V.

Notes p.49 continue It+6 → V4/3/V → V6 → i. In four parts, V4/3/V → V6 forces the 7th (C) onto B♮ while the bass also rises to B♮, doubling the leading tone. The example uses root-position V; please check the intended voicing.
Burstein (Ch. 31) also says the German sixth "usually" (not always) goes through the cadential 6/4.
